summary: Reviews password-authenticated key agreement (PAKE) schemes, which let two parties use a weak shared password to authenticate each other and derive strong cryptographic keys. It describes the different kinds of schemes and gives requirements and recommendations for designers of new ones. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: Two friends share a short secret word. A PAKE lets them prove they both know it and make a much stronger secret code, without anyone listening in learning the word.

questions: how do pake schemes prevent offline attacks
subtitle: Guidelines for designing secure password-based authentication protocols.

tldr.problem: Passwords are easy to use but weak, so directly using them in cryptographic exchanges is risky. Brute-force dictionary attacks can easily guess them during key exchange.
tldr.mechanism: PAKE schemes let two parties prove they both know a shared password and derive a strong cryptographic key, without the password itself being sent or guessed offline.
tldr.outcome: The document reviews different types of PAKE schemes and provides requirements for designers of new ones, produced by the IRTF Crypto Forum Research Group.

today: RFC 8125 is an Informational RFC published by the Crypto Forum Research Group and is not on any standards track. It remains the consensus design guidance for PAKE schemes and is referenced by cryptography researchers and protocol designers when developing password-authenticated systems.

sections.title: Why Password Authentication Matters
sections.content:
Passwords are the most widely used method of authentication on the Internet, largely because they are intuitive and easy for users to enter repeatedly. However, passwords tend to be weak and guessable—users choose them to be memorable, which makes them vulnerable to brute-force dictionary attacks where an attacker tries common words and variants until one works.

A Password-Authenticated Key Agreement (PAKE) attempts to solve this problem by constructing a cryptographic protocol that allows two parties to authenticate each other and derive a strong shared encryption key using only a weak shared password. The crucial property is that the password is never sent over the network, and an attacker cannot perform an offline brute-force attack to guess it; they must actively interact with one party for each guess.
sections.eli5: A password is easy to guess if you keep trying every word. A PAKE makes the attacker talk to you for every guess, so they get caught quickly.

sections.title: Two Flavors of PAKEs
sections.content:
PAKE schemes come in two main varieties based on how the password is stored.

In a balanced PAKE, both parties store the same representation of the password (either the password itself with a salt, or a password element in a finite field). Balanced PAKEs are useful when either party can initiate the connection or both can initiate simultaneously, such as in mesh networking or Internet of Things applications where devices need symmetric relationships.

In an augmented PAKE, one party (typically the client) knows the raw password while the other party (typically the server) stores a transformed version computed with a one-way function. This offers an advantage: if an attacker obtains the server's stored credentials, they cannot directly impersonate clients to other servers; they must first crack the individual passwords through a brute-force attack. Augmented PAKEs are well-suited to strict client-server protocols such as Transport Layer Security (TLS).
sections.eli5: In balanced PAKEs, both friends memorize the word the same way. In augmented PAKEs, one friend remembers the word and the other remembers a code that came from it—safer if the code gets stolen.

sections.title: How PAKEs Prevent Offline Attacks
sections.content:
The fundamental security property of PAKE schemes is that an eavesdropper or offline attacker cannot efficiently verify password guesses without interacting directly with one of the parties in the exchange.

PAKEs achieve this through different mechanisms. Some schemes (such as Encrypted Key Exchange, EKE) use symmetric encryption derived from the password to encrypt an ephemeral public key; only someone with the correct password can decrypt it. Others (such as SPEKE and J-PAKE) exchange unencrypted public key values alongside password-derived values, so that if the passwords match, both parties can compute a common secret, but mismatched passwords lead to different results. A third approach (used in PACE) encrypts a nonce rather than a key, using it to generate the base for key agreement.

In all cases, an attacker's only viable strategy is repeated online guessing—attempting the protocol with each password candidate and checking whether the exchange succeeds or whether the final derived keys match. This limits the attacker to one guess per interaction, and detection becomes possible after a small number of failed attempts.
sections.eli5: The password is mixed into the math in a way that you have to guess-and-check by actually talking to the other side. After a few wrong guesses, they'll notice you're not a real friend.

sections.title: Critical Design Considerations
sections.content:
PAKE designers must address several technical and practical challenges.

Security proofs are essential. Each PAKE scheme should come with a formal security proof in a well-defined mathematical model, clearly stating its assumptions and the hardness problems (such as discrete logarithm) it relies on. This foundation allows users to trust the scheme.

Implementation attacks are a real threat. Even a mathematically sound scheme can leak information through side channels—timing variations in the computation, power consumption, or electromagnetic emissions can reveal secret values. Designers should discuss how to implement their scheme in constant time to prevent timing attacks, and for schemes running on devices like smart cards, how to protect against physical attacks.

Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) presents special challenges. Many PAKE schemes work naturally with finite field elements, but ECC-based schemes require mapping random strings to points on a curve, and sometimes mapping curve points back to strings indistinguishable from random data. Designers must carefully specify or define these mappings with implementation security in mind.
sections.eli5: The designers need to prove the math works, make sure no snooping through timing can break it, and explain how to use it with fancy curve math.

sections.title: Applications and Variants
sections.content:
PAKEs are often building blocks in larger protocols rather than standalone schemes. The choice of balanced or augmented PAKE depends on the protocol's structure: augmented is better for strict client-server relationships, while balanced fits protocols where either side can initiate.

Several interesting variants exist. Password-Authenticated Key Distribution allows a party to retrieve a key from a secure repository using a password for authentication. Another variant enables two parties to exchange public keys using a PAKE instead of certificates, allowing a short one-time code to be transformed into a long-term public key pair. Yet another combines password-based authentication with certificate-based authentication by using a certificate's private key to blind the password agreement process.

Group PAKEs extend the concept to multiple parties, either through constructions that convert any two-party PAKE to a group version, or by using a trusted server that shares a password with each participant separately.
sections.eli5: PAKEs are tools other protocols use. They can work for sharing keys from a safe box, for turning a short code into a long-term key, or for groups of friends instead of just two.
